title: National Income Accounting
outcomes: Explain the meaning, compilation and uses of national income estimates.
Distinguish and inter-convert GDP, GNP, NDP, NNP at market prices and factor cost, national income, personal and disposable income, and use the GDP deflator.
Measure national income by the value added, income and expenditure methods and know what is included and excluded.
Describe India's regional accounts and explain why GDP is not a full measure of welfare, and the limitations of national income computation.

meta.exam_tip: Numerical MCQs on aggregates appear every attempt. Learn the three switches (depreciation, NFIA, NIT), watch the signs of NFIA and net exports, and remember operating surplus = rent + interest + profit.

concepts.title: National income accounting — meaning, who compiles it, why it matters
body: National income accounting is the set of macro-economic accounts that traces the economy from production of goods and services through to their final use. It defines the concepts (GDP, NNP and so on) and builds measures for them. It was pioneered by Simon Kuznets and Richard Stone, both Nobel laureates.

In India the national accounts are compiled by MoSPI's Central Statistical Organisation (CSO) (MoSPI = Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation); State Directorates of Economics and Statistics (DESs) compile State Domestic Product. (Real-world note: in 2019 the CSO and NSSO were merged into the National Statistical Office (NSO) within MoSPI; the study material uses the name CSO, so answer "CSO" if that is the option offered.)

Uses: (i) businesses use it to forecast demand; (ii) it shows the structure of income by sector and how that structure shifts over time; (iii) government uses sectoral data to frame sector-specific policies; (iv) it gives a quantitative base for macro-economic models and for assessing policies; (v) it throws light on income distribution and allows ratios such as investment, tax or fiscal deficit to GDP; (vi) international comparisons of income and living standards help decide eligibility and terms for loans and aid; (vii) combined with monetary data it guides policy on growth and inflation.
concepts.analogy: National accounts are the economy's financial statements: GDP is the "turnover", depreciation the wear and tear, NNP the "net" figure.
concepts.work: Equity analysts, bankers and CFOs read GDP releases to forecast demand; CAs use nominal GDP growth as a sanity check on a client's revenue projections.

concepts.title: GDP — nominal, real and the GDP deflator
body: Gross Domestic Product at market prices (GDP MP) is the market value of all final goods and services that are produced inside a country's domestic territory over a period (usually a year), before deducting depreciation. Only final goods are counted, to avoid double counting.

Nominal GDP (GDP at current prices) values output at the prices of the same year, so it can rise because output rises or because prices rise. Real GDP (GDP at constant prices) values output at the prices of a chosen base year, so it changes only with quantities.

GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100. It is a price index: it is 100 in the base year; above 100 means prices are higher than in the base year. Real GDP = Nominal GDP ÷ deflator × 100, and Nominal GDP = Real GDP × deflator ÷ 100.
Inflation between two years = (Deflator in year 2 − Deflator in year 1) ÷ Deflator in year 1 × 100. If the deflator falls from one year to the next, the price level has fallen.
concepts.analogy: Nominal GDP is your salary in rupees; real GDP is what that salary can actually buy.
concepts.work: When a client reports 12% revenue growth in a year of 7% inflation, the CA points out that real growth is only about 5% — the deflator logic applied to a company.

concepts.title: Gross vs net, domestic vs national
body: Gross vs net: the difference is depreciation (consumption of fixed capital). Net = Gross − Depreciation. So NDP MP = GDP MP − Depreciation.

Domestic vs national: the difference is net factor income from abroad (NFIA). National = Domestic + NFIA. GNP MP = GDP MP + NFIA. NFIA = factor income earned by our residents abroad − factor income earned by non-residents in our territory = net income from property and entrepreneurship + net compensation of employees + net retained earnings of resident companies abroad.

GDP counts what is produced inside the country by anyone; GNP counts what is earned by the country's normal residents anywhere. Profit of a foreign company's factory in India is in India's GDP but in its home country's GNP.
NNP MP = GNP MP − Depreciation = NDP MP + NFIA = GDP MP + NFIA − Depreciation. If NFIA is positive, GNP > GDP; if negative, GNP < GDP.
concepts.analogy: Domestic = "made in India"; national = "made by Indians". The gap between them is NFIA.
concepts.work: For countries with large remittance or profit outflows, the gap between GDP and GNP changes the picture of income available to residents — relevant in sovereign-risk and country-risk notes.

concepts.title: Market price, factor cost and basic price
body: Market price and factor cost differ by net indirect taxes (indirect taxes − subsidies). Market price = Factor cost + Indirect taxes − Subsidies; Factor cost = Market price − Indirect taxes + Subsidies.
GDP FC = GDP MP − NIT. Built up from incomes it equals CoE + OS + mixed income + depreciation, where OS (operating surplus) is rent, interest and profit taken together.

Basic price sits in between: Basic price = Factor cost + Production taxes − Production subsidies; Market price = Basic price + Product taxes − Product subsidies. Product taxes (like GST) are levied per unit of product; production taxes (like land revenue, stamp duty, professional tax) are paid because of production activity, not per unit. So market price includes both kinds of taxes and excludes both kinds of subsidies. India reports gross value added (GVA) at basic prices.
concepts.analogy: Factor cost is what the cook, the landlord and the owner receive; market price is what you pay at the counter after GST and before any subsidy.
concepts.work: CAs see the same idea in company accounts: revenue is shown net of GST because indirect tax is collected for the government, not earned by the firm.

concepts.title: National income and related aggregates
body: NDP FC = sum of factor incomes earned in the domestic territory = CoE + OS + mixed income. It is also called domestic (factor) income.
National income = NNP FC = factor income of normal residents = NDP FC + NFIA. If NFIA > 0, national income exceeds domestic factor income.
Per capita income = GDP (or national income) ÷ population — a rough indicator of living standards.

Personal income (PI) is the current income actually received by households (including non-profit institutions serving households) from all sources, earned or not. PI = NI + incomes received but not earned (transfer payments such as pensions, scholarships, unemployment allowance, interest on national debt) − incomes earned but not received (undistributed corporate profits, corporate tax, employers' social-security contributions, government's income from property and entrepreneurship and savings of non-departmental enterprises). National income is therefore not the sum of personal incomes.
Disposable personal income (DI) = PI − personal direct taxes − other compulsory payments (fees, fines). It is what households can consume or save.

Private income = private sector's factor income from NDP + NFIA + interest on national debt + net transfers from the rest of the world + current transfers received from government. Net National Disposable Income = NNI + other net current transfers from abroad; Gross National Disposable Income = NNDI + depreciation.
concepts.analogy: National income is what the family earned; personal income is what actually reached the family's hands; disposable income is what is left after paying income tax.
concepts.work: Consumer-goods firms track personal disposable income, not GDP, when forecasting household spending.

concepts.title: Circular flow and the three methods
body: Production, distribution and disposition go on together: firms produce using factor services (production phase); they pay rent, wages, interest and profit to households (distribution or income phase); households spend that income on consumer and investment goods (expenditure or disposition phase), which calls forth more production.

So national income can be measured three ways: as the sum of value added (product method — shows the contribution of each producing sector); as the sum of factor incomes (income method — shows the share of each factor); and as the sum of final expenditure (expenditure method — shows consumption and investment). In principle all three give the same figure, and each acts as a check on the others.

In India no single method is used throughout: value added (production) method in agriculture, income method in the small-scale (unorganised) sector, and expenditure method in construction. The income method suits economies where incomes are well recorded through tax returns.
concepts.analogy: Count the money in a closed room three ways — as it is made, as it is paid out, as it is spent — and you should get the same total.
concepts.work: Revenue assurance in a company follows the same idea: reconcile production records, payroll and sales — three views of one activity.

concepts.title: Value added (product) method
body: Step 1: identify producing enterprises and classify them into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors (and sub-sectors).

Step 2: find gross value added at market prices: GVA MP = Value of output − Intermediate consumption, where Value of output = Sales + Change in stock (closing − opening). If total purchases are given, imports are already in intermediate consumption; if domestic sales are given separately, exports must be added.
Step 3: Σ GVA MP = GDP MP; less depreciation = NDP MP (net value added); less net indirect taxes = NDP FC; plus NFIA = national income.

Include: own-account production of fixed assets, imputed value of production for self-consumption, imputed rent of owner-occupied houses and change in stocks. Exclude: intermediate goods (to avoid double counting), sale of second-hand goods (only the dealer's commission is counted), and purely financial transactions.
concepts.analogy: Wheat → flour → bread: count only what each stage adds, not the full price at every stage, or the wheat is counted three times.
concepts.work: The same "value added" idea underlies GST: tax is effectively paid on the value added at each stage.

concepts.title: Income method
body: Also called the factor payment or distributed-share method: add the factor incomes paid by all producing units in the domestic territory. NDP FC = CoE + OS + mixed income, with OS made up of rent, interest and profit; national income = NDP FC + NFIA.

Compensation of employees covers basic pay, DA, bonus and commission, the employer's PF and social-security contribution, and perks given in kind (at imputed value). Profit = corporate tax + dividends + retained earnings. Rent includes imputed rent; royalty is included.

Exclude: transfer incomes (pensions, scholarships, gifts), capital gains and windfall gains, proceeds from selling used goods or shares and bonds, spending out of past savings, interest the government pays on public debt, interest households pay on loans taken for consumption, and inter-firm interest. Include commissions, brokerage and imputed value of owners' services.
Mixed income: for the self-employed (lawyers, doctors, traders, farmers), labour and capital income cannot be separated, so the combined income is recorded as mixed income.
concepts.analogy: Open every producer's cash book and add only the payments made to the people who provided land, labour, capital and enterprise.
concepts.work: Tax data (salary TDS, business returns) feed the income method, which is why better tax compliance improves the quality of national income estimates.

concepts.title: Expenditure method
body: Also called the income disposal approach: GDP MP = sum of final expenditure = Private final consumption expenditure (PFCE) + Government final consumption expenditure (GFCE) + Gross domestic capital formation (GDCF) + Net exports (X − M).

PFCE: purchases of final goods and services by households and non-profit institutions serving households, including produce for own consumption and payments for domestic services; purchase of land and new houses by households is not consumption — it is capital formation. GFCE: since government services (defence, administration, public health) are not sold, they are valued at the cost of providing them; transfer payments (pensions, scholarships, unemployment allowance) are excluded.

GDCF = gross fixed capital formation (machinery, equipment, construction, own-account production of capital goods) + change in stocks + net acquisition of valuables (jewellery, works of art). Gross = net + depreciation.
From GDP MP: GNP MP = GDP MP + NFIA; NNP MP = GNP MP − depreciation; NNP FC = NNP MP − NIT.
concepts.analogy: Add up every final bill paid in the economy — by families, government, businesses buying machines, and foreigners buying our exports — and take away what we spent on imports.
concepts.work: Budget documents and RBI reports discuss "private consumption" and "investment rate" (GDCF/GDP) — the expenditure-side components a CA must read fluently.

concepts.title: The system of regional accounts in India
body: Almost all states and union territories estimate state income and many estimate district income. State income, or Net State Domestic Product (NSDP), is the money value of all goods and services produced within the state in a year, counted without duplication. Per capita state income = NSDP ÷ mid-year projected population of the state.
The State Income Units within each State DES prepare the estimates, with the CSO advising on concepts and methods.

Activities that cut across state boundaries — railways, communications, banking and insurance, central government administration — are called supra-regional sectors. They are estimated for the country as a whole and allocated to states using suitable indicators.
concepts.analogy: Each state keeps its own "branch accounts"; head-office items that serve all branches (railways, banks) are allocated by a key.
concepts.work: State-wise GSDP and per capita income guide location decisions, state finance commission work and credit-rating of state government bonds.

concepts.title: GDP and welfare; limitations of national income computation
body: GDP is not a full measure of welfare. It ignores: the distribution of income (two countries with equal per capita income can differ greatly in well-being); quality improvements from new technology and management; hidden or illegal production; most non-market production and non-economic contributors such as health, education and political participation; the loss of leisure; economic "bads" such as crime, pollution and congestion; unpaid volunteer work; fairness, gender equality and community security; externalities; and the difference between output that makes us better off and output that only prevents us from becoming worse off (e.g. more police spending due to rising crime, or repair bills after accidents, both raise GDP).

Conceptual difficulties: no agreed definition of national income; separating final and intermediate goods; treatment of transfer payments; services of durable goods; incorporating income distribution; valuing new goods at constant prices; valuing government services.

Practical challenges (especially in developing countries): inadequate and unreliable data; a large non-monetised sector; production for self-consumption; incomes not recorded because of illiteracy and ignorance; lack of proper occupational classification; and estimating depreciation accurately.
concepts.analogy: GDP is a speedometer: it tells you how fast the car is going, not whether the passengers are comfortable or where the car is heading.
concepts.work: ESG and sustainability reporting, increasingly assured by CAs, exists precisely because profit and GDP miss externalities like pollution.

jobs.title: Is our growth real?
jobs.role: CA in industry — strategy and planning
jobs.situation: The CEO wants to tell investors that sales grew 14% last year "far ahead of the economy". The latest data show nominal GDP growth of 11% and real GDP growth of 7%.
steps: Compare like with like: company sales are nominal, so compare 14% with nominal GDP growth of 11%, not with real growth of 7%.
Estimate the company's own price increase (say 5%) to find its real volume growth (about 9%).
Present both: nominal outperformance of 3 points and real outperformance of about 2 points.
Note that the gap between nominal and real GDP growth gives the economy-wide inflation implied by the deflator.
jobs.takeaway: Always match nominal with nominal and real with real — the GDP deflator is the bridge.
jobs.think: Approximately what inflation does the GDP deflator imply here?
jobs.answer: About 4% — roughly the gap between 11% nominal and 7% real growth (more precisely 1.11/1.07 − 1 ≈ 3.7%).

jobs.title: Choosing a state for a new plant
jobs.role: CA in practice advising a mid-size manufacturer
jobs.situation: The client is comparing three states for a new consumer-durables plant and warehouse.
steps: Collect GSDP growth, per capita NSDP and the share of manufacturing and services from the State DES releases.
Use per capita income as a proxy for local purchasing power, but remember it hides income distribution.
Combine with state incentive schemes, logistics and labour data.
Flag data limits: supra-regional activities (railways, banking) are allocated to states by indicators, so state figures are estimates.
jobs.takeaway: Regional accounts help location decisions, but per capita figures are averages and hide distribution.

mcqs.q: National income accounting was pioneered by:
mcqs.explain: Both received the Nobel prize for their work on national accounts.

mcqs.q: In India, national accounts statistics are compiled by:
options: The Central Statistical Organisation in MoSPI
mcqs.explain: The CSO (MoSPI) compiles national accounts, as per the study material; State DESs compile state income. (Since 2019 the CSO is part of the National Statistical Office, NSO.)

mcqs.q: GDP at market prices includes:
mcqs.explain: GDP is gross of depreciation and domestic (excludes NFIA).

mcqs.q: Nominal GDP is ₹4,500 crore and real GDP is ₹3,600 crore. The GDP deflator is:
mcqs.explain: 4,500 ÷ 3,600 × 100 = 125: prices are 25% above the base year. 80 is the ratio inverted.

mcqs.q: Real GDP is ₹600 crore and the price index (deflator) is 125. Nominal GDP is:
mcqs.explain: Nominal = Real × deflator ÷ 100 = 600 × 1.25 = ₹750 crore.

mcqs.q: Nominal GDP is ₹2,400 crore and the deflator is 160. Real GDP is:
mcqs.explain: Real = Nominal ÷ deflator × 100 = 2,400 ÷ 1.6 = ₹1,500 crore.

mcqs.q: The GDP deflator was 140 last year and 147 this year. The inflation rate is:
mcqs.explain: (147 − 140) ÷ 140 × 100 = 5%. 7% is the point change, not the percentage.

mcqs.q: If nominal GDP is less than real GDP in a year, the GDP deflator is:
options: Below 100 — prices lower than in the base year
mcqs.explain: Deflator = Nominal/Real × 100 < 100.

mcqs.q: The basis of distinction between "gross" and "net" is:
mcqs.explain: Net = Gross − consumption of fixed capital.

mcqs.q: The basis of distinction between "national" and "domestic" is:
mcqs.explain: National = Domestic + NFIA.

mcqs.q: GDP MP is ₹8,200 crore, NFIA is (−) ₹150 crore and depreciation ₹700 crore. NNP MP is:
mcqs.explain: NNP MP = GDP MP + NFIA − Dep = 8,200 − 150 − 700 = ₹7,350 crore. ₹7,650 adds NFIA with the wrong sign.

mcqs.q: Profit earned in India by a branch of a foreign company is included in:
options: India's GDP but not India's GNP
mcqs.explain: Produced inside India (domestic) but earned by a non-resident (deducted in moving to national).

mcqs.q: Market price and factor cost differ by:
mcqs.explain: MP = FC + indirect taxes − subsidies.

mcqs.q: GDP MP is ₹5,000 crore, indirect taxes ₹600 crore and subsidies ₹150 crore. GDP FC is:
mcqs.explain: GDP FC = 5,000 − 600 + 150 = ₹4,550 crore. ₹4,250 deducts subsidies instead of adding.

mcqs.q: Basic price equals:
options: Factor cost + production taxes − production subsidies
mcqs.explain: Then market price = basic price + product taxes − product subsidies.

mcqs.q: National income is:
mcqs.explain: NI = NNP FC = NDP FC + NFIA.

mcqs.q: NDP FC is ₹6,400 crore and NFIA is ₹120 crore. National income is:
mcqs.explain: NI = NDP FC + NFIA = 6,400 + 120.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is added to national income to arrive at personal income?
mcqs.explain: Transfers are received but not earned; the other items are earned but not received (deducted) or already in NI.

mcqs.q: Disposable personal income equals:
options: Personal income − personal direct taxes − other compulsory payments
mcqs.explain: DI is what households can spend or save.

mcqs.q: Personal income is ₹4,800 crore, personal income tax ₹520 crore and fines/fees ₹30 crore. Disposable personal income is:
Which phase of the circular flow involves spending of factor incomes on consumption and investment goods?
mcqs.explain: Production → distribution (factor incomes) → disposition (expenditure).

mcqs.q: Value of output in an industry is calculated as:
mcqs.explain: Change in stock = closing − opening; then GVA = value of output − intermediate consumption.

mcqs.q: Sales ₹900 crore, opening stock ₹120 crore, closing stock ₹80 crore, intermediate consumption ₹400 crore. GVA MP is:
mcqs.explain: Value of output = 900 + (80 − 120) = 860; GVA = 860 − 400 = ₹460 crore. ₹540 adds the fall in stock instead of deducting it.

mcqs.q: Which of these is included in national income?
mcqs.explain: Imputed rent is a service produced; the others are transfers or exchanges of existing assets.

mcqs.q: Under the income method, which of the following is excluded?
mcqs.explain: Interest on public debt is treated as a transfer payment.

mcqs.q: Mixed income of the self-employed means:
options: Combined factor income that cannot be separated into labour and capital income
mcqs.explain: Typical of farmers, traders, professionals.

mcqs.q: PFCE ₹3,000 crore, GFCE ₹900 crore, GDCF ₹1,100 crore, exports ₹400 crore, imports ₹550 crore. GDP MP is:
mcqs.explain: 3,000 + 900 + 1,100 + (400 − 550) = ₹4,850 crore. ₹5,950 adds imports instead of deducting.

mcqs.q: In the expenditure method, purchase of a new house by a household is treated as:
mcqs.explain: Land and residential buildings bought by households are part of capital formation.

mcqs.q: Government expenditure on scholarships is:
options: Excluded from GFCE as a transfer payment
mcqs.explain: Transfers create no production in return.

mcqs.q: Activities like railways, banking and central government administration, whose output cannot be assigned to one state directly, are called:
mcqs.explain: They are estimated nationally and allocated to states using indicators.

mcqs.q: Per capita state income is obtained by dividing NSDP by:
options: The mid-year projected population of the state
The number of workers in the state
mcqs.explain: Per capita NSDP uses the state's mid-year population.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a reason why GDP is an imperfect measure of welfare?
options: It ignores income distribution and economic "bads" such as pollution
mcqs.explain: GDP misses distribution, leisure, externalities, unpaid work and more.

mcqs.q: Increased spending on police because of a rise in crime:
options: Raises GDP although it only prevents people from becoming worse off
mcqs.explain: GDP does not separate output that improves welfare from output that only prevents a decline.

mcqs.q: A "resident unit" for GDP purposes means a unit:
options: With its predominant economic interest in the country's economic territory for one year or more, whatever its nationality
Located only in India with Indian owners
Composed of citizens living in India
mcqs.explain: Residence depends on centre of economic interest, not nationality.

remarks: A step-wise table makes the sequence clear and earns method marks.
tips: Remember the three switches: gross/net (depreciation), domestic/national (NFIA), MP/FC (NIT).

checks.label: GDP MP = CoE + OS + MI + CFC + NIT

questions.q: For a firm (₹ crore): sales 820; opening stock 90; closing stock 60; intermediate consumption 310; depreciation 45; indirect taxes 70; subsidies 20. Calculate GVA MP, NVA MP and NVA FC.

scheme.pt: Value of output with change in stock

remarks: A fall in stock reduces the value of output — many candidates add it.
tips: Write "change in stock = closing − opening" with its sign.

questions.q: Compute national income by the expenditure method and by the income method (₹ crore): PFCE 2,600; GFCE 700; net domestic capital formation 560; depreciation 140; net exports (−) 80; net indirect taxes 210; NFIA 30; compensation of employees 1,900; rent 250; interest 300; profit 650; mixed income 470.

model.text: Both methods give the same national income.

remarks: Strong answers show both methods side by side and note that they agree.
mistakes: Using NDCF instead of GDCF in GDP.
Forgetting NFIA in the income method.
tips: Expenditure method gives GDP MP first; income method gives NDP FC first.

summary: GDP MP: value of final output produced inside the domestic territory in a year, before depreciation.
Gross − Depreciation = Net; Domestic + NFIA = National; Market price − NIT = Factor cost.
NI = NNP FC = CoE + OS + Mixed income + NFIA.
PI = NI + transfers received − incomes earned but not received; DI = PI − direct taxes − compulsory payments.
GDP deflator = Nominal ÷ Real × 100; inflation = change in deflator ÷ previous deflator × 100.
Three methods: value added, income, expenditure — India uses a mix.
State income = NSDP; supra-regional sectors allocated by indicators.
GDP ignores distribution, non-market work, leisure, bads and externalities.
remember: Value of output = Sales + (closing − opening stock).
GDP MP = C + G + GDCF + (X − M); GDCF = NDCF + depreciation.
Basic price = FC + production taxes − production subsidies; MP = basic price + product taxes − product subsidies.
traps: Second-hand goods, shares, transfer payments and interest on public debt are not in national income.
Operating surplus already includes rent, interest and profit.
A fall in stock reduces value of output.
NI is not the sum of personal incomes.

quickref.v: NNP FC = NDP FC + NFIA = CoE + OS + MI + NFIA
Sales + change in stock − intermediate consumption
PI = NI + transfers − earned-not-received; DI = PI − direct taxes

viva.model: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced inside the country's domestic territory in a year, whether by residents or non-residents. GNP is GDP plus net factor income from abroad, so it measures what the country's normal residents earn wherever they produce. The difference between the two is net factor income from abroad.

viva.q: What is the GDP deflator and how is it calculated?
viva.model: The GDP deflator is a price index that measures the current price level compared with the base year. It is calculated as nominal GDP divided by real GDP, multiplied by 100. It is 100 in the base year, and dividing nominal GDP by the deflator and multiplying by 100 gives real GDP.

viva.q: What is the difference between market price and factor cost, and how do you convert one into the other?

viva.q: Name the three methods of measuring national income and what each adds up.
viva.model: The three methods are the value added or product method, the income method and the expenditure method. The value added method adds the net value added by all producing units, that is value of output minus intermediate consumption. The income method adds factor incomes — compensation of employees, operating surplus and mixed income. The expenditure method adds final expenditure — private and government final consumption, gross domestic capital formation and net exports.

viva.q: How is personal income derived from national income, and what is disposable income?
viva.model: Personal income equals national income plus incomes received but not earned, such as transfer payments and interest on national debt, minus incomes earned but not received, such as undistributed corporate profits, corporate tax and social security contributions. Disposable income is personal income minus personal direct taxes and other compulsory payments; it is what households can consume or save.

viva.q: Why is GDP not a perfect measure of welfare?
viva.model: GDP ignores how income is distributed, so the same per capita income can mean very different well-being. It leaves out non-market and voluntary work, the value of leisure, and quality improvements. It does not deduct economic bads like pollution, crime and congestion, or other externalities, and it even rises with spending that only prevents us from becoming worse off, such as more police spending or accident repairs.
